title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration fixed shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates. The preregistered hypotheses (H1, H2) about comparative generator/repair robustness were therefore preregistered but unobserved under the shared_candidate execution semantics; we document artifact evidence that rules out prompt/response contamination, and we show per‑task validator traces that explain why the repair subsystem was never invoked.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, absence of transient safety violations) while allowing expressive intents across vendor CLIs. Two canonical architectures are (A) translation‑first pipelines that constrain generation to a vendor DSL and apply formal verification/solvers, and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair.

This study asked, preregistered, and executed the following head‑to‑head question: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation): (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design with N = 120 paired tasks, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and paired_binary_analysis_v1 as the analysis executor.

A decisive preregistered design choice was shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired task the system generated a single LLM candidate once and supplied that identical candidate to both downstream arms. This design intentionally removes generator variance from the confirmatory estimand and reduces the measured quantity to validator‑acceptance parity for identical textual candidates. The original preregistered hypotheses H1 and H2 (stating differences in success rate and repair coverage between architectures) therefore remained preregistered but unobserved under the shared_candidate execution; this manuscript reports the measured estimand (validator‑acceptance parity) and the artifact evidence that explains the execution outcomes and rules out contamination.
sections.related_work: Prior work falls into two complementary traditions: formal translation→verification systems that emphasize constrained output spaces and deterministic guarantees [10,11,5], and recent LLM‑driven agentic NetOps research that emphasizes flexible generation plus iterative repair and verifier‑guided self‑correction [3,4]. Translation‑first systems use DSLs and solver/verification tooling to bound generator variance and provide counterexamples; LLM‑centric evaluations typically exercise independent generator sampling, instrument repair iterations, and measure repair coverage and transient unsafe‑proposal rates. Our study differs methodologically by holding the generator output fixed per pair (shared_initial_candidate) to measure downstream validator‑acceptance parity, producing an orthogonal, operationally relevant comparison useful when operators consider swapping validators or orchestration stacks while preserving candidate proposals.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and execution contract. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) and execution contract froze: paired design (120 task pairs), generator = gpt‑5‑mini, deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, shared_initial_candidate semantics, maximum_model_calls = 240, and analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 (bootstrap percentile CIs and exact McNemar).

Task generation and prompt instrumentation. Confirmatory tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task manifest entry archived the natural‑language intent, constraints, canonical reference answer, and a required_sequence. For transparency, three representative intents (verbatim from execution/task_manifest.jsonl) are: (1) task‑000001 intent — “Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up. Do not modify any other interface.”; (2) task‑000002 intent — “Move service from uplink1 to uplink2. At least one of the two uplinks must remain admin up at every step, so enable uplink2 before shutting down uplink1. Preserve all MTU and VLAN settings and do not touch other interfaces.”; (3) task‑000003 intent — “Change the point‑to‑point pair edge1/edge2 to matching MTU 1800. Both interfaces must be down before either MTU change, and both must finish admin up. Preserve both VLANs and every setting on the uplinks and mgmt1.” Each of these intent texts appears verbatim in the archived task_manifest entries (execution/task_manifest.jsonl).

What was sent to the model and contamination controls. For each pair the provider call record (execution/provider_calls/task‑<id>‑shared‑initial.json) contains the exact prompt delivered to gpt‑5‑mini: the immutable master prompt (archived: provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 recorded in the bundle) plus the task‑specific intent and constraints from the task manifest. Representative provider_call artifacts are archived at execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json (and analogous paths for other tasks); these full provider_call JSONs are the canonical record of model input. Execution accounting and provider audit confirm execution isolation: analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json reports cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false and hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, consistent with one independent generation per pair and no cross‑pair prompt leakage.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and orchestration. Orchestration created one shared LLM generation per task pair and distributed that identical candidate to both downstream arms. Execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). The shared_initial_provider_trace_path fields in per‑task scoring JSONs point to the provider_call entries that record the exact prompt and the model response used by both arms.

Deterministic validator and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion and ordering (make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), final state checks, and a boolean validation_after.valid. A scoring success (1) required validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scorer traces are archived under execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json and contain normalized_response, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, repair_applied flag, and the validator id/version. The preregistered repair configuration permitted bounded repair (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) and the transformation_manifest (execution/transformation_manifest.json) and orchestration logs record that the repair subsystem was available though unused in this run.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary numerical outcomes. Execution completed all preregistered confirmatory episodes: completed_episode_count = 240, complete_pair_count = 120, failed_episode_count = 0. Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cache_miss_count = 120 (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json). The analysis contingency is n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Marginal success rates: baseline = 120/120 = 1.0; guarded = 120/120 = 1.0. The paired difference A − B = 0.00; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numbers are deterministic consequences of the degenerate contingency table and are reported exactly as archived in analysis/results.json.

Representative per‑task validator diagnostics and why repairs were not invoked. The per‑task scoring artifacts demonstrate the mechanical reason repairs were not applied: the shared LLM candidates satisfied the validator's required command and ordering checks for these examples. Representative archived scoring JSONs show the following actual values:
• execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validation_after.valid = true, repair_applied = false; normalized_configuration = "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up".
• execution/scoring/task-000002-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 2, required_command_count = 2, validation_after.valid = true, repair_applied = false; normalized_configuration = "interface uplink2 admin up\ninterface uplink1 admin down".
• execution/scoring/task-000003-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 6, required_command_count = 6, validation_after.valid = true, repair_applied = false; normalized_configuration = "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge2 admin down\ninterface edge1 mtu 1800\ninterface edge2 mtu 1800\ninterface edge1 admin up\ninterface edge2 admin up".

These representative traces (and the full cohort of execution/scoring/*.json artifacts) show parsed_command_count == required_command_count and validation_after.valid == true for accepted candidates; consequently the repair subsystem (configured per preregistration with maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 and available in the transformation manifest) was never triggered and repair_applied remains false across all episodes. Aggregation across scoring artifacts yields repair_applied count = 0 and is reflected in analysis/condition_summary.csv.

Contamination, missingness, and reproducibility diagnostics. Contamination checks flagged no items (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty). Missingness diagnostics report complete_pairs = 120 and zero failures (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). The execution and analysis artifacts (execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/responses/*.txt, execution/provider_calls/*.json, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/*) together constitute the canonical reproducible record of inputs, prompts, responses, validator traces, and analysis outputs.
sections.discussion:
Measured estimand versus original hypotheses. Because the preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics, the reported confirmatory estimand measures validator‑acceptance parity: given identical textual LLM candidates, do downstream orchestration and verification paths differ in deterministic validator acceptance? The observed perfect concordance (n11 = 120) answers this restricted question in the negative: both validators accepted the identical candidates for every pair. The preregistered hypotheses H1 and H2 — which posit differences in independent generator success rates and repair coverage between architectures — were preregistered but unobserved under the shared_candidate execution semantics and therefore remain empirically untested here.

Artifact‑grounded account of concordance. The scoring artifacts show that the shared candidates often matched canonical reference answers after normalization and ordering adjustments; parsed_command_count equaled required_command_count in representative tasks and validators returned validation_after.valid = true. The provider_call artifacts (execution/provider_calls/task‑<id>‑shared‑initial.json) record that prompts contained only the immutable master prompt plus the task intent and constraints (excerpts of which are quoted in Methods); no canonical reference strings were injected into those prompts. Provider audit and execution isolation logs confirm no cross‑pair prompt leakage.

Design implications and follow‑up protocol modifications. To test the originally preregistered generator/repair hypotheses the preregistration must be altered to exercise independent generator variance and repair instrumentation: (i) disable shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives independent LLM draws (initial model_calls_used rises from 120 to 240); (ii) permit multiple independent samples per arm to estimate generator variance; (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied > 0 becomes observable and secondary estimands (repair coverage, mean repair iterations) are measured. Each change would produce clear, archived signatures (higher hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_provider_trace_path entries in scoring JSONs, and nondegenerate paired_contingency_table.csv) and is practical under the existing adapter and orchestration.

Operational interpretation and cautions. Validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates indicates that, under the chosen validator and emulator, swapping orchestration/validation stacks need not change deterministic acceptance outcomes when candidates are identical. This is an informative operational check for validator replacements but is not evidence that either architecture produces safer or more robust proposals when operating autonomously with independent generation. Practitioners should therefore treat validator‑parity as a necessary but not sufficient condition for architectural interchangeability; independent sampling and repair evaluations remain essential.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifactized paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks deterministic validators accepted identical LLM candidates in both arms for every pair (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false across scoring artifacts); therefore preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage and independent generator robustness remain preregistered but unobserved in this execution. We provide an artifact bundle with provider_call records (execution/provider_calls/*.json), per‑task scorer traces (execution/scoring/*.json), and analysis artifacts (analysis/*) that together document the measured estimand, rule out prompt contamination for representative tasks, and specify minimal preregistration modifications required to exercise the originally intended generator/repair comparisons.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures (H1/H2 were preregistered but unobserved under this execution).

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
